title: A Deserted Wife Is Brought Home
overview: The LORD speaks to Jerusalem, pictured as a childless, abandoned wife after the exile in Babylon, and promises to take her back, fill her with children, and keep her safe for good.

parts.label: The childless woman sings (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Jerusalem, emptied when its people were taken captive to Babylon, is pictured as a woman who never had children, now told to celebrate because her family will grow huge. She must make her tent bigger to hold them all, and the line about taking over other nations and their empty cities reflects the hopes and conflicts of that time.

parts.label: Taken back after shame (vv. 4-8)
parts.note: The exile is pictured as a young wife sent away, and the LORD as the husband who calls her home; many readers take the 'shame of your youth' as the people's past unfaithfulness. The text openly says God turned away in anger, but calls it brief next to a kindness that lasts forever.

parts.label: A promise like Noah's (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: After the flood in Genesis, God swore never to flood the earth again, and here he makes a similar sworn promise not to turn his anger on his people again. Even if mountains shift, his loyal love and his promised peace will not.

parts.label: A city built of jewels (vv. 11-14)
parts.note: The battered city is promised rebuilding with gleaming stones, a picture of beauty and safety, though the exact gems are uncertain because the old words are hard to identify. Her children will be taught by the LORD, a line Jesus quotes in John 6:45, and Christians read the jeweled city of Revelation as echoing this picture.

parts.label: No weapon will win (vv. 15-17)
parts.note: If anyone attacks, it will not be God sending them, and the attackers will end up surrendering. Since God made both the weapon maker and the destroyer, no weapon against his people will succeed, and in this courtroom picture every accuser loses while God declares his servants in the right.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether these promises belong mainly to the Jewish people and Jerusalem, perhaps with a fulfillment still to come, or are fulfilled in the church, with many holding some form of both.
think: Can a relationship that has been through a real break ever become closer than before, and what would it take for that to happen?
